text:
Taki the Brewer was still asleep, although the sun’s rays had long since pierced the windows of his stuffy little room, clouded with grime; the rays gradually lit up his feet, crept toward his belly, gleamed on his dried and cracked lower lip, scorched by the inner fire, rushed into his open mouth, and penetrated to the throat from which the waves of a disturbing snore were issuing. Just at that time the postman knocked three times on the door. But does Taki’s ear understand such gentle signals? If it had been a weekday—well and good, but it happened to be a holiday. On a holiday, you know, a person lets himself go a little more: he clinks glasses with this one, clinks with that one, and before you know it, he has had a bit too much. And the same thing happened to Uncle Taki: out of a desire to recommend his beer, he had quite soaked himself. My point is, so to speak, that you should not be surprised that the postman repeated the knocking on the door, and when no one answered, he delivered such merciless blows upon the entirely innocent door that, even if a whole cauldron of beer had visited Uncle Taki’s stomach, he would still have woken up. And he did wake up. He opened his eyes, squinted against the sun, and in a voice worthy of the throat from which it came, he asked:

— Who’s there?

— Mail — replied the postman, entered the room, stepped up to the bed, handed over a letter, and hastened to escape the stifling atmosphere of the unventilated bedroom.

Uncle Taki coughed a little, as was proper, rubbed his eyes, and unfolded the letter.

An invitation!

“Honorable Sir, you are respectfully requested to come tomorrow, Sunday, at 5 o’clock in the afternoon, to the warehouse “Suhindol Wines,” where the question of founding a temperance society will be discussed.
With respect: For the initiators, Tanas Dochoolu, innkeeper“

My God! How timely this invitation came. For old Taki’s parched throat and cracked lips, there were at that moment such advocates in favor of temperance that he enthusiastically embraced the noble idea, and all that remained was for the fifth hour after noon to strike, so that he could declare himself the most ardent defender of temperance. During the day, old Taki drank water. (To be honest, let’s speak straight—he did drink two little glasses of wine, but that’s just how it’s said.) Whether five o’clock had struck or not, old Taki crossed the threshold of the spacious warehouse “Suhindol Wines.”
— Is Uncle Tanas here? - he asked the boy who was standing behind the counter.
— Please come in, they’re here, in the little room — the boy replied respectfully and stepped aside to open the little door for him.

The host, Tanas Dochoolu, greeted his fellow kindly and invited him to take a seat. Solidly and silently, several citizens sat along the walls, inspired and drawn here by the noble idea of the future society. Bay Taki greeted them all, and silence was restored again, broken only by modest coughs. It was clearly seen that those gathered were expecting someone, without whom they did not dare open the meeting. Not much time passed before the outer door opened. Dochoolu hurried out to see whether the desired guest was coming, but immediately returned with a dissatisfied look. Into the room burst quite unexpectedly Danko Harsazina. “We’ve struck gold!” whispered Bay Tanas to Bay Taki. It was clear that this was not the expected person. Danko opened his mouth to say something—what would Danko’s conversation be like: to curse someone; but no one showed any desire to listen to him, and he fell silent. A few more minutes passed and (thank God!) the boy rushed headlong into the room and cried out in alarm: “He’s coming! He’s coming!”
Everyone stood up. The outer door opened and on the threshold appeared, in all his grandeur, in the flesh, our mutual friend Bay Ganyo Balkanski.
— Oh! Long live it! — exclaimed the long-awaited guest enthusiastically, without specifying which “long live it,” but without explanation everyone understood that this referred to the future society.

— Long live! — responded the gathered group, and they began taking turns shaking hands with Bay Ganyo. Danko Harsuzina, always less delicate, even dared (imagine!) to pat Bay Ganyo on the neck, but Mr. Balkanski shot him such a look that Danko tucked his tail between his legs and huddled in a corner. “Don’t hold it against him, Bay Ganyo,” the host whispered, “you know what he’s like. Danko is just Danko — a roughneck.”

The meeting opened. Ah, gentlemen, if only you had had the good fortune to attend that gathering! As soon as those very Bay Ganyo mouths opened, was it a man speaking, or a nightingale singing... Wouldn’t he convince you, Bay Ganyo? Why, not just about a society, but he could even persuade you to believe that your father is Musala and Vitosha is your mother... Never mind. Everyone was convinced that this was exactly the right time to found a temperance society; only Danko the Rascal — would you believe it — was a complete doubting Thomas. Well, they spoke this way and that way, but no — he sat in the corner, kept smirking under his mustache, and tossed out some skeptical little remark now and then. “It is time now to... such-and-such —” Dochoolu orated, “to found... this-and-that... you understand, a society...” And Danko let out a “well, then.” “Drunkenness, esteemed gentlemen,” Bay Taki went on, “has a bad effect on our work, our health, our offspring...” “Nonsense!” whispered Danko, smirking under his mustache. But even without a rooster, dawn breaks! There was no way they were going to abandon the lofty idea because of one Danko. They left Danko to twirl his mustache and set about constituting the society. They decided to name the society “Temperance,” and to ask the schoolmaster to write them a charter. The schoolmaster, whether he liked it or not, had to write the charter, because, if you ask me, he was the first to light the fuse for this society. For the time being, the initiators limited themselves to electing, as has been customary since time immemorial, an executive committee. They elected: Bay Ganyo, of course, as chairman; Tanas Dochoolu, as the landlord, vice-chairman; and Bay Taki as treasurer. Done! Has there ever been an election that did not end with a treat? Impossible. That’s how it has always been, that’s how it is, and that’s how it will go on. The vice-chairman, as host, was the first to make amends — he called the boy and whispered to him: “Two kilos of the old stuff, quickly!” The wine was brought. But wine — is that wine, this one from Suhindol? Crystal clear, the devil take it!...
— Well then, cheers, may it be auspicious!
— Long live the chairman, hurrah!
— Thank you, long live His Royal Highness and the esteemed government!
— Hooray!
— Down with drunkenness!...
Bai Ganyo was shamed too. Bai Taki was shamed too. And they repeated... and repeated again... and so on until nightfall...

It was already dark when I was walking with my companion along “Clean Work” Street. As we passed by the Suhindol Wines warehouse, an unusual noise coming from inside drew our attention and aroused our curiosity. We went into the warehouse and, through the little window of the inner room, this is the scene that flashed before us: most of those gathered were snoring, sprawled without order on the chairs; old Taki, with his arms crossed over his paunch, was snorting heavily, his head drooping and his eyes half-open; a thin, tall gentleman, in a worn frock coat and blue spectacles, was turning in all directions and shouting into space: “I am against machines, whatever anyone may say, but I am against machines.” Dochoolu was sitting at the table, his boy was holding a candle, and he was writing down the bill in the notebook with a trembling hand. Bay Ganyo was striking the table with all his might and, with a savage look, was shouting: “Me? I’ll prove it to them, I’ll make them understand who old Ganyo is...” And Danko Harsuzina, inspired by this energetic tone, had fixed his eyes on Bay Ganyo and seemed to be asking him with his eyes: “Well, say, Bay Ganyo, say, brother, whom should I grab by the throat, whom should I kick out the door?...”
The boy went out with the candle.
— Boy, what is this company? - my companion asked.
— Society Against Drunkenness — answered the boy.
If there were prizes for the most carefree laughter to the point of delight, then my comrade and I would have received first prize at that moment.
Sofia, 12 May 1895.
